title: A framework to identify dispersal and establishment constraints in restoration: Freshwater macroinvertebrates as an illustrative example
content:
In restoration practice, initial state assessment is often insufficient to identify specific limiting factors, with practitioners resorting to off-the-shelf restoration methods which may not be appropriate. In the case of lotic invertebrate communities, the tools to comprehensively assess communities do exist; we need to improve understanding and accessibility to practitioners to champion use of these tools in restoration. Through targeted use of different invertebrate sampling methods (e.g. kick sampling, Surber sampling, light trapping, drift sampling), our framework provides an assessment of potential limiting factors for dispersal and establishment that will allow for more strategic restoration methods, with higher chances of success.


Abstract

Given the growing awareness of human-induced degradation of ecosystems, substantial efforts are being made to rehabilitate degraded ecosystems. However, there is considerable uncertainty regarding the ability of these degraded systems to recover. Despite long-term calls for a greater focus on monitoring, both planning and evaluation of restoration are rarely underpinned by relevant data. Where ecological communities have become depauperate, colonisation processes must be supported to facilitate community recovery. Colonisation comprises the physical arrival of an organism into an area (dispersal) and its subsequent successful establishment within the local community. Both dispersal and establishment are influenced by biological traits, local habitat conditions and landscape context. We introduce a novel framework to systematically identify dispersal and establishment-related constraints on the recovery of communities, using macroinvertebrate communities in lotic systems as an illustrative example. The framework incorporates targeted monitoring tools, including drift sampling and aerial adult surveys, to distinguish dispersal from establishment limitations and inform appropriate interventions. By systematically assessing dispersal and establishment, the framework can be used to identify suitable restoration actions. For example, measures to facilitate dispersal (such as riparian area management or translocations), or measures to support establishment (such as improving water quality and instream habitat availability) may be prioritised. Synthesis and applications: In practice, initial state assessment is often insufficient to identify specific limiting factors, with practitioners resorting to off-the-shelf restoration methods which may not be appropriate. In the case of lotic invertebrate communities, the tools to comprehensively assess communities do exist; we need to improve understanding and accessibility to practitioners to champion use of these tools in restoration. Through targeted use of different invertebrate sampling methods (e.g. kick sampling, Surber sampling, light trapping, drift sampling), our framework provides an assessment of potential limiting factors for dispersal and establishment that will allow for more strategic restoration methods, with higher chances of success.
